scenes.title: Key ideas
scenes.vo: Many on-chain perp exchanges let you deposit into a liquidity vault that acts as the counterparty to traders (the "house"). The vault earns trading fees, borrowing/funding fees and part of liquidations, and loses when traders win. First, Returns: fees + traders' losses minus traders' profits. Next, Risks: a run of profitable traders (or a few very large ones), open interest concentrated on one side, oracle manipulation or latency, the market-making strategy of the vault (some vaults actively trade), and exchange contract risk. And finally, Check: the vault's historical P and L split (fees versus trader P and L), its open-interest caps, how it prices assets (oracle), and withdrawal rules (cooldowns, fees).

scenes.vo: Let's work an example, step by step. A vault shows 25% A.P.R.: 18% from fees, 7% from traders' net losses over the last 6 months. In a strong one-directional trend, traders who are long win, so the vault's "trader P and L" component can swing to minus 20% or worse, wiping out the fees. Size it as an active trading exposure, not as fixed income, and check whether withdrawals are delayed in stress.

scenes.q: When does a perp liquidity vault lose money?
scenes.a: When traders are net profitable, e.g. in strong trends.
